narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and worked in your favor, pushing the prediction toward passing. However, your first-year and third-year law school grades pulled much more strongly in the opposite direction. These two academic performance measures were the dominant reasons the model concluded you were more likely to fail than to pass.

Your first-year grades placed you in the second decile, far below the average of sixth decile among accepted students. Similarly, your third-year grades also ranked in the second decile, compared with an average around the sixth decile for those who were admitted. These consistently low class rankings outweighed the benefit of your LSAT score and led the model to forecast a slightly higher risk of bar exam failure.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.3 was also well below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, and choosing full-time work while studying is the path taken by over 90% of admitted students, so these details did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class ranking through targeted study and consider retaking the LSAT if you can increase your score meaningfully. Strengthening your academic record now will directly address the factors that caused this rejection. (248 words)
